faq.q: Why is GCS preferred over simple ‘alert‑verbal‑pain‑unresponsive’?

faq.q: Can a normal blood glucose rule out hypoglycaemic coma?

exam: A 7‑year‑old with fever and coma in a malaria‑endemic area – what is the next immediate step? — Check blood glucose, give IV glucose if <2.8 mmol/L, then start artesunate while arranging rapid malaria test.

A patient with GCS 7 and unequal pupils – what does this indicate and how should you act? — Fixed dilated pupil suggests brain herniation; secure airway, raise head of bed, and arrange urgent neuro‑imaging or neurosurgical referral.

How do you differentiate cerebral malaria from bacterial meningitis in a comatose patient? — Malaria often has recent malaria exposure, anaemia, and negative meningeal signs; meningitis shows neck stiffness, CSF pleocytosis; both need empiric treatment if uncertainty persists.

Why is a single dose of benzodiazepine preferred for seizure control in hepatic failure? — It terminates the seizure quickly with minimal hepatic metabolism; phenobarbital would accumulate and worsen encephalopathy.
What are the key components of a serial neurological monitoring chart? — GCS, pupil size/reactivity, motor strength grading, seizure activity, and any new focal signs recorded at least hourly.
When is it safe to withhold anticoagulation in a patient with suspected stroke? — If intracranial bleed cannot be excluded (e.g., abnormal CT or papilledema), anticoagulation must be delayed.
Explain why a normal CT does not rule out early ischaemic stroke. — Early CT may miss cytotoxic oedema; clinical deficits guide thrombolysis decisions when imaging is unavailable.

What preventive measures reduce the incidence of neurological deterioration in sickle‑cell disease? — Regular transfusion programs, hydroxyurea, malaria prophylaxis, and prompt treatment of infections.
ai.title: Neurological Status Assessment
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Neurological status is the bedside evaluation of consciousness, motor and sensory function, and seizures. It guides urgent decisions, tracks disease progression, and alerts to life‑threatening complications, especially where diagnostics are limited.

b: Use the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) to quantify consciousness (E‑V‑M scores).
Pupils: size, symmetry, and light reaction indicate brainstem function.
sections.p: In the ATLS and routine ward round, ‘disability’ refers to the neurological status: level of consciousness, pupil size/reactivity, motor strength, and seizure activity.

b: Mild: GCS 13‑15, no focal deficit.
Moderate: GCS 9‑12, may have focal weakness.
Severe: GCS ≤8, often with abnormal pupils or seizures.
sections.p: Severity is staged by GCS and presence of focal deficits.

b: Infections: cerebral malaria, bacterial meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, HIV encephalopathy.
Metabolic: severe hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbances, renal or hepatic encephalopathy.
Vascular: intracerebral haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke, hypertensive encephalopathy.
Toxins: herbal poisons, organophosphates, alcohol withdrawal.
sections.p: Identify reversible and common tropical causes before rare etiologies.

b: Confusion → early sign of metabolic or infectious encephalopathy.
Lethargy or coma → severe metabolic derangement or intracranial bleed.
Focal weakness or cranial nerve palsy → stroke or space‑occupying lesion.
Seizures or asterixis → hepatic encephalopathy, severe acidosis.
sections.p: Presentation varies with the underlying cause but follows a pattern of altered consciousness, focal weakness, and/or seizures.

t.b: What is the current level of consciousness? – Guides urgency and need for airway protection.
Is there brainstem compression? – Fixed, dilated pupil suggests herniation.
Is hypoglycaemia causing altered mental status? – <2.8 mmol/L requires immediate glucose.
Are electrolytes or renal failure contributing? – Correct severe hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia.

t.a: Malaria rapid test or thick smear
t.b: Is cerebral malaria present? – Positive test in febrile patient with coma mandates artesunate.
Is meningitis likely? – CSF pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein guide antimicrobial choice.
Is there a bleed or mass? – Contra‑indicates lumbar puncture and may need neurosurgery.

b: GCS ≤8 with airway compromise.
Unreactive pupils or new anisocoria.
New focal deficit with rapid progression.
Seizure refractory to first‑line benzodiazepine.
sections.p: Recognise signs that demand immediate escalation.

b: Airway: intubate if GCS ≤8 or unable to protect airway; maintain cervical spine protection.
Seizures: give IV benzodiazepine (e.g., diazepam) – avoid phenobarbital in severe hepatic failure.
Infection: start empiric antimalarials for cerebral malaria; give ceftriaxone for bacterial meningitis if resources allow.
Metabolic: correct glucose, electrolytes, and acid‑base disturbances promptly.
Avoid: routine anticoagulation until intracranial bleed ruled out; avoid high‑dose steroids without clear indication.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the airway, and prevent secondary injury.

b: Re‑assess GCS, pupils, and motor strength every hour in the first 24 h.
Treat malaria prophylactically in endemic areas; ensure HIV patients are on ART.
Educate on safe herbal medicine use and avoidance of organophosphate exposure.
sections.p: Serial neurological checks and addressing modifiable risk factors reduce mortality.

b: Psychiatric agitation – lacks focal deficits and abnormal pupils.
Severe dehydration – improves rapidly with fluid replacement, no focal signs.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic altered consciousness but have different management.

b: Normal CT early after head injury does not exclude evolving bleed.
Negative malaria rapid test in low‑parasitaemia; confirm with thick smear.
sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.

whenToSeekHelp: GCS ≤8, airway compromise, or fixed dilated pupil
New focal neurological deficit with rapid decline
Seizure lasting >5 minutes or recurrent without recovery
